title: Explicit Instruction Is Having a Moment
author: Groshell, Zach
summary: Zach Groshell announces and summarizes a new essay for the American Enterprise Institute and researchED making the cumulative case for explicit instruction, built on his own training, the research literature, and decades of classroom evidence. He directly rebuts three common caricatures: that explicit instruction is just teacher talk, that it kills problem-solving and creativity, and that it damages self-esteem, countering each with findings from Project Follow Through and related research. The piece argues explicit instruction was the only Project Follow Through model to produce positive gains in higher-order thinking. Groshell closes by arguing that the students most often denied explicit instruction are those labeled 'struggling' or 'at-risk,' who have the least margin for instructional experimentation.
points: Project Follow Through found Direct Instruction was the only model tested that produced positive gains in higher-order thinking, undercutting the claim that explicit teaching suppresses problem-solving.
A well-run explicit lesson is highly interactive, not simply 'the teacher talking' — this caricature doesn't match how explicit instruction is actually implemented.
Self-esteem follows competence, not the reverse: success at real tasks builds confidence, so shielding struggling students from explicit instruction to protect their self-esteem backfires.
Students labeled 'struggling,' 'low,' or 'at-risk' are the ones most harmed by romantic, discovery-oriented teaching methods and have the least room for instructional error.
Explicit instruction should be the default plan from the start for at-risk students, not a late intervention added after years of ineffective teaching.
quotes: Explicit instruction is just the teacher talking." It isn't. A well-run explicit lesson is one of the most interactive things you'll see in a classroom.
Direct Instruction was the only Project Follow Through model to produce positive gains in higher-order thinking.
Children feel good about themselves when they can actually do things. Success drives motivation, not the other way around.
The children we call "struggling," "low," or "at-risk" are the children most consistently harmed by the romantic forms of teaching I was trained to practice.
Explicit instruction shouldn't be written into their intervention plans after we've wasted years of their schooling. It should have been the plan all along.
